latest.title: Building Customer Loyality for Marning Corn in Bulukumba: The Impact of Brand Image, Service Quality, and Product Quality on Purchase Decisions and Customer Satisfaction
latest.venue: Journal of Global Innovations in Agricultural Sciences
latest.abstract: Marning corn products, typical food, and souvenirs from the Bulukumba district are packaged simply without complete product information. Yet by integrating well-designed packaging with clear and relevant product information that can improve product quality, brands can improve the overall consumer experience, build trust, and foster long-term loyalty. This research aims to analyze the direct and indirect influence of brand image, service quality, and product quality on purchasing decisions and consumer satisfaction on consumer loyalty to making corn. The research method used quantitative analysis with structured interview techniques using a sample of corn buyers in Bulukumba Regency. The data analysis used is structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis using the AMOS application. The research results show that consumer satisfaction and brand image have a significant direct influence on loyalty. Brand image and service quality have an impact on purchasing decisions. Product quality, service quality, and brand image influence consumer satisfaction. Meanwhile, the variables of service quality and production quality do not have a significant effect on consumer loyalty through purchasing decisions and consumer satisfaction as intervening variables of brand image, service quality, and production quality. Increasing income in the Morning Corn business can be achieved by prioritizing brand image, service quality, and product quality so that later it can increase the number of buyers and increase consumer loyalty. Keywords: Customer loyalty, buying decision, customer satisfaction, brand image, service quality, product quality and marning corn.

latest.title: Coping with sustainability information overload: The role of generative artificial intelligence literacy
latest.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science- Economics and Business Administration
latest.abstract: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations

latest.title: The impact of environmental knowledge on water waste in restaurants on complaining behavior intention: The mediating role of perceived motivation and skepticism
latest.venue: Journal of Tourism Leisure and Hospitality
latest.abstract: This study aims to examine the impact of environmental knowledge about water waste in restaurants on consumers' intentions to complain, while also elucidating the mediating roles of perceived motivation and skepticism in this relationship. A scenario-based experimental research design was employed, and data were gathered from 388 restaurant goers through an online survey. Participants were randomly assigned to two restaurant scenarios: one in which water-saving practices were not observable and another in which they were prominently displayed. The data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrapped mediation analyses in SPSS 26 and AMOS 23. The research findings demonstrate that, in the first scenario—characterized by the absence of visible communication about water conservation—environmental knowledge had no direct, significant influence on the intention to display complaint behavior. Environmental knowledge increased perceived motivation and skepticism. Perceived motivation did not directly and significantly influence the intention to engage in complaint behavior; however, skepticism increased the intention to engage in such behavior. In the second scenario, where water-saving methods were visible, environmental knowledge directly and positively affected the intention to complain, perceived motivation, and skepticism; furthermore, perceived motivation and skepticism partially mediated the relationship between environmental knowledge and the intention to complain. The findings suggest that restaurants must not only implement eco-friendly practices but also communicate them to consumers in a transparent, visible, and trustworthy way. In this context, restaurant managers should create informative visuals and communication strategies that promote water

latest.title: From sustainability practices to consumer behaviour: a PLS-SEM analysis of sustainable packaging adoption in the FMCG food sector
latest.abstract: Growing environmental concerns and plastic waste are driving the need for sustainable packaging solutions for the FMCG food sector. Understanding consumer attitude and purchasing behavior for sustainably packaged food products is crucial for promoting sustainable practices. This study assesses the association between the 5R's sustainability practices, consumer attitude, purchase intention, and actual purchasing behavior towards sustainably packaged FMCG food products. Primary data were collected from 210 consumers using the purposive sampling method from various hypermarkets in Coimbatore city. The data were analysed by Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling with SmartPLS 4 software. From the results, it is revealed that 5R sustainability practices significantly influence consumer attitude (β = 0.730) towards sustainably packaged food products. Furthermore, consumer attitude has a positive influence on purchase intention (β = 0.666), whereas purchase intention considerably influences actual purchasing behavior (β = 0.543). However, the direct association between attitude and actual purchasing behavior was not significant (β = −0.115), indicating the existence of an intention–behavior gap in sustainable consumption. The structural model explains 53.3% of the variance in attitude, 44.4% in purchase intention, and 22.5% in actual purchasing behavior, highlighting that purchase intention acts as a key mediating factor between attitude and actual behavior. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening consumer intention and improving the availability of sustainably packaged food products to enhance actual purchasing behaviour

latest.title: Internalization of Halal Lifestyle Values in The Use of Syass Glow Body Lotion Among Young Muslim Women in Pinrang
latest.venue: Journal of Economics Law and Humanities
latest.abstract: Background/Introduction: The growing awareness of Islamic values highlights the importance of halal lifestyles in cosmetic consumption, particularly among young Muslim women influenced by beauty standards, social environments, and digital marketing. Research Objectives: This study examines the understanding and internalization of halal lifestyle values and their influence on the consumption of Syass Glow body lotion among young Muslim women in Tadokkong, Pinrang. Methodology: Using a qualitative descriptive approach, data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. Data analysis involved reduction, display, and conclusion drawing, guided by halal lifestyle, Maqashid al-Shariah, and consumer decision-making theories. Results: The findings indicate that participants have a basic understanding of halal lifestyles, which is not consistently reflected in their consumption practices. Social media and peer influence play a greater role in shaping consumption behavior than religious and family education. From a Maqashid al-Shariah perspective, these practices do not fully reflect the preservation of religion (hifz al-din), life (hifz al-nafs), intellect (hifz al-'aql), and wealth (hifz al-mal). Purchasing decisions are primarily driven by the desire for brighter skin, affordability, peer recommendations, and social media promotions rather than halal considerations. Unique Contribution: This study reveals a gap between understanding of the halal lifestyle and actual cosmetic consumption practices, contributing empirical insights into Islamic consumer behavior from a Maqashid al-Shariah perspective. Conclusion: It highlights the need to strengthen halal literacy and consumer awareness through religious education and consumer protection initiatives.

latest.title: Green Human Resource Management and Environmental Performance in Tanzanian Local Government Authorities: The Role of Green Organizational Culture and Organizational Citizenship Behaviour towards Environment
latest.venue: Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education
latest.abstract: This study investigated the effect of Green Human Resource Management on Environmental Performance in Tanzanian Local Government Authorities (LGAs) with a focus on the mediating effect of Green Organisational Culture and the moderating effect of Organisational Citizenship Behaviour toward Environment.A quantitative research design was adopted, and the study was conducted among employees of Tanzanian LGAs.Respondents were selected using stratified and simple random sampling techniques.A total of 400 questionnaires were given out, 231(57.8%) of which were completed and used for analysis.Data were analysed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM), using Smart-PLS 4. Findings showed that Green Human Resource Management had a positive effect on Environmental Performance.Furthermore, the findings show that the relationship between Green Human Resource Management and Environmental Performance is positively and significantly mediated by Green Organisational Culture.This implies that a green organisational culture enhances the effect of Green Human Resource Management on environmental performance.The findings also showed that Organisational Citizenship Behaviour toward Environment positively and significantly moderates the relationship between Green Human Resource Management and Environmental Performance, meaning that the positive effect of Green Human Resource Management on environmental performance is stronger when employees engage in higher levels of voluntary environmental behaviour.The study recommends LGAs to improve Green Human Resource Management functions for better environmental performance.LGAs should also improve green organisational culture and promote environmental citizenship behaviour of employees to maximise the environmental benefits a

latest.title: The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets
latest.abstract: Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. latest.title: Brand recommendations by generative AI chatbots: A comparative analysis in consumer decision-making
latest.abstract: This study explored the algorithmic gatekeeping role of generative AI chatbots in consumer decision-making. Using algorithmic content analysis and an audit design, it examined the brand recommendations of the three most widely used chatbots in Türkiye: ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot. Four product categories were selected by crossing involvement level and consumption motivation: detergent, chocolate, smartphone and an international holiday. Each prompt was submitted once to each model in a neutral and an emotional version, and the resulting 24 responses were coded descriptively. Neutral prompts mostly elicited technical and functional arguments, whereas emotional wording shifted the persuasion frame toward emotional appeals in 8 of 12 responses; predominantly emotional responses appeared only in hedonic categories. In the holiday category, all three models framed even the neutral prompt in romantic terms. The models typically offered three to ten brands rather than a single one, yet ChatGPT stated a first-person preference in every response and displayed priced shopping cards in five of eight. The findings suggest that generative AI can act as an intermediary that shapes brand visibility and has the potential to steer consumer preferences, raising questions for marketing ethics and large language model optimization.

latest.title: Outcome versus process focused future thinking: results from a randomised experiment
latest.abstract: Objectives Future thinking plays a central role in emotion and behaviour, yet different modes of simulation may have distinct effects. This pre-registered experiment compared outcome- and process-focused future thinking on affective and cognitive responses to imagined events. It was hypothesised that anticipated pleasure, anticipatory pleasure and positive affect would be higher in an outcome-focused task relative to a process-focused task. Further, ratings of perceived control and likelihood of the future event will be higher after a process-focused task relative to the outcome-focused.Methods Participants (N = 134; M = 35.1 years (age), SD = 13.1) generated personally relevant future events online, were randomly assigned to focus on either outcomes or the steps required to achieve them, and completed pre-post questionnaires relating to these future events.Results Outcome-focused thinking increased anticipatory pleasure, motivation and personal significance. In contrast, process-focused thinking reduced perceived control and was associated with reductions in both anticipated and anticipatory pleasure. No effects were observed for perceived likelihood, and positive affect increased modestly across conditions.Conclusions These findings indicate that outcome-focused future thinking enhances affective engagement, whereas process-focused thinking may introduce constraints that attenuate perceived control and reward-related responses. Distinguishing between these modes of future thinking has implications for models of motivation and interventions targeting future-oriented cognition.

latest.title: SMART RETAILING IN INTERNET COMMERCE: AN AI-ENABLED CUSTOMER-CENTRIC SERVICE FRAMEWORK
latest.venue: EPH - International Journal of Business & Management Science
latest.abstract: This conceptual paper examines AI-enabled smart retailing as a customer-facing service transformation in Internet commerce rather than as a narrow technological or operational innovation. Drawing on a selective, theory-driven synthesis of services marketing, smart retailing, AI-enabled marketing, customer experience, service-dominant logic, human–AI interaction, and responsible-AI research, it develops a three-layer framework linking AI-enabled service capabilities, customer-experience mechanisms, and Internet-commerce outcomes. The framework identifies three capability groups—algorithmic personalisation and decision support, AI-mediated service interaction, and predictive service intelligence—and four evaluative mechanisms: decision value, interaction quality, transaction confidence, and algorithmic legitimacy. These mechanisms shape customer satisfaction, engagement, service-recovery effectiveness, platform trust, relationship quality, continuance intention, value co-creation, and inclusive service value. Human–AI governance, including privacy protection, transparency, fairness, customer control, human review, and digital accessibility, is treated as a boundary condition that determines whether AI-enabled services are perceived as trustworthy and customer-centred or as intrusive, opaque, unfair, and exclusionary. The paper contributes to Internet-commerce research by repositioning AI as a service-enabling capability and by explaining how customer evaluations translate AI applications into commercial and relational outcomes. It also proposes a focused research agenda for empirical testing across e-commerce websites, mobile applications, online marketplaces, social-commerce platforms, and omnichannel systems.

latest.title: Self-pleasure vs conformity: understanding Chinese Gen Z consumption behaviors in the smart electronics market
latest.venue: Young Consumers Insight and Ideas for Responsible Marketers
latest.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explain how Chinese Generation Z consumers construct preferences by moving between conformity and self-pleasure across a digitally mediated smart-appliance journey. Design/methodology/approach An abductive qualitative design combines 48 in-depth interviews (16 each for smart kitchen appliances, floor-mopping robots and smart toilets) with consumer journey mapping. Self-determination theory, conformity theory, social comparison theory and constructive consumer choice guide cross-case interpretation. Findings Retrospective accounts suggest a transition consistent with comparison-mediated internalization. Social cues first reduce uncertainty; social comparison can then convert visible choices into personally relevant benchmarks. Research and use build competence and perceived fit, allowing autonomy and experiential satisfaction to become more influential. Post-purchase sharing satisfies relatedness and renews social influence. Two category attributes shape the path: decision risk/technical complexity and social visibility/identity expressiveness. Practical implications Brands should use credible social proof for discovery, comparison support for evaluation, reliable experiences for use and context-appropriate advocacy mechanisms after purchase. Originality/value The study distinguishes the roles of conformity, social comparison and self-determination within a process model and identifies category conditions associated with differences in reported movement from external referencing to self-endorsed choice.

latest.title: Beyond resistance: deinfluencing, consumer activism and the incorporation of critique on digital platforms
latest.abstract: Deinfluencing is a social media trend where content creators advise audiences not to buy ‘must-have,’ overhyped, overpriced, low-quality, or unnecessary products. It serves as a potential form of resistance to the logic of overconsumption. Gaining momentum on TikTok in early 2023, deinfluencing rapidly spread across social media platforms where the meanings and norms of consumption are publicly negotiated and can acquire collective relevance. This conceptual paper proposes a critical reading of the phenomenon, arguing that deinfluencing does not necessarily constitute a negation of influencer marketing, but may instead be incorporated into the commercial arrangements it contests while retaining critical meanings and effects. Situated at the intersection of consumer culture, consumer activism, influencer marketing and platformisation, the paper examines the infrastructural and commercial conditions through which consumer critique acquires visibility and value. It develops a multilevel conceptual model comprising three analytically distinct but potentially overlapping mechanisms through which critical discourse can be incorporated into influencer marketing: substitution , at the content level, whereby criticism of particular products redirects rather than rejects consumption; hybridisation , at the level of practices, whereby influencing and deinfluencing coexist within creators’ communicative repertoire; and authenticity renewal , at the level of audience relations, whereby rejecting some products can strengthen creator credibility and, under certain conditions, the persuasive value of subsequent endorsements. Platformisation conditions the circulation and visibility of these critical practices without determining their effects. Drawing on the sociological concept of bou

latest.title: The affideme: How consumers inhabit worlds amid epistemic plurality
latest.abstract: Belief is often approached as conviction, error, or identity. We examine believing instead as practical continuation: how consumers keep a contested orientation workable when certainty is unavailable and competing standards of plausibility coexist. Drawing on qualitative research on complementary and alternative therapeutic practices in France, we follow engagements sustained while biomedical authority remains acknowledged. We introduce the affideme as a minimal comparative configuration in which heterogeneous supports make further involvement practicable under such conditions. An affideme is identifiable within a focal episode when a contestable support acquires practical consequence, connects with at least one other support, and the resulting orientation remains usable alongside acknowledged counter-warrants. Embodied traction, interpretive legibility, and projective capacity describe how supports contribute to this viability. Across trajectories, affidemes can strengthen, recalibrate, desynchronise, fail to form, be reabsorbed into stronger biographical or institutional frames, or close when uncertainty is resolved or displaced. The concept helps Consumer Studies compare how contested, market-mediated worlds remain inhabitable without full conviction.

latest.title: Exploring the Key Drivers of Online Purchasing Behaviour for Organic Food Products
latest.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
latest.abstract: The growing consumption of organic food products, coupled with the rapid expansion of digital commerce, has significantly transformed consumer purchasing behaviour. The present study examines the key factors influencing consumers’ online purchasing behaviour towards organic food products, based on primary data collected from 200 respondents in Hyderabad city. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire designed to assess consumer perceptions across the pre-purchase, purchase, post-purchase, and other influencing dimensions. Descriptive statistics and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) were employed to analyse the data and identify the major determinants of online purchasing behaviour. The findings indicate that time efficiency in obtaining product information is the most important consideration during the pre-purchase stage, while delivery time is the leading determinant during the purchase stage. In the post-purchase phase, customer service support emerges as a crucial factor influencing consumer satisfaction and retention. The Exploratory Factor Analysis identifies five underlying dimensions: timeliness, price and certification, trustworthiness, serviceability and innovativeness. Together, these factors explain 64.04% of the total variance, highlighting their importance in shaping consumers’ online purchasing decisions. The findings offer valuable insights for online retailers and organic food marketers in developing customer-oriented marketing strategies.

latest.title: The relationship between brand ethicality and brand trust: brand credibility, emotional attachment, and perceived quality effects
latest.abstract: Introduction The purpose of this research was to explore the relationship between brand ethicality and brand trust. Specifically, we developed a conceptual model which proposes that brand credibility has a moderating effect on the relationship between brand ethicality and brand trust, and that perceived quality and emotional attachment have mediating effects on brand trust. Methods We tested the conceptual model by conducting a 2 × 2 (low versus high brand ethicality and low versus high brand credibility) between-subjects experiment, with brand trust as the dependent variable. Data ( N = 208) were collected at a large university in Bangladesh, and were analysed using PLS-SEM. Results Results of the experiment suggest that brand ethicality has a direct effect on brand trust. Brand ethicality also enhances emotional attachment and perceived quality, which, in turn, lead to increased brand trust. Brand credibility, however, does not have a moderating effect on the relationship between brand ethicality and brand trust. Discussion Drawing on signalling theory, the findings provide causal evidence that brand ethicality builds brand trust through two parallel pathways: an affective pathway via emotional attachment and a cognitive pathway via perceived quality. Contrary to expectations, brand credibility did not act as a boundary condition, suggesting that brand ethicality and brand credibility may be better understood as sequential antecedents of brand trust rather than as interacting constructs. For practice, marketers ought to increase brand ethicality to increase brand trust, both directly and via emotional attachment and perceived quality.

latest.title: Consumer decision in online processed-food purchase: income, price, and digital quality perception
latest.venue: Journal of Agribusiness in Developing and Emerging Economies
latest.abstract: Purpose This study analyzes the association of consumer income with online processed-food demand through digital quality perception and perceived price on digital food platforms in Makassar, Indonesia. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a cross-sectional online survey of 162 female household food decision-makers. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling in International Business Machines Statistical Package for the Social Sciences Analysis of Moment Structures, with bias-corrected bootstrapping used to assess the indirect association. Findings Consumer income was positively associated with perceived price, but not with digital quality perception or online processed-food demand. Digital quality perception was positively associated with perceived price and online processed-food demand, whereas perceived price was not directly associated with demand. The indirect association was positive but not statistically significant. The model explained 56% of the variance in online processed-food demand. Research limitations/implications The single-city purposive sample and cross-sectional design limit causal interpretation and statistical generalizability. Future studies should use longitudinal, multisource, or platform-based transaction data. Social implications Reliable digital product information can support informed consumer choice and strengthen trust in developing-economy e-commerce. Originality/value This study provides developing-market evidence that platform-based quality cues are the closest correlates of online processed-food demand, while price plays a limited direct role.

latest.title: Promotion-rule Complexity and Checkout Abandonment in E-commerce Sales Events: The Mediating Role of Consumer Confusion
latest.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
latest.abstract: With the rise of big e-commerce sales events, multiple layers of promotions exist, such as platform coupons, store coupons, stacking, membership discounts and category discounts, which make the checkout process more complex. Promotional mechanisms can help to make the product more attractive, but can also diminish price transparency and add to cognitive load. This research examines the relationship between promotion-rule complexity and consumer checkout abandonment tendency and the role of consumer confusion in this relationship. A mixed-method approach was adopted to analyze a publicly available dataset of 12,330 online shopping sessions, and a survey based on a set of scenarios with 218 valid responses. The findings show that the complexity of the promotion rule has a significant effect on consumer confusion, which consequently results in a higher checkout abandonment tendency. Promotion-rule complexity is positively related to checkout abandonment through consumer confusion. The results contribute to the promotion literature by focusing on the last mile of the promotion process and have implications for e-commerce platforms that aim to minimise the friction involved in decisions by creating simpler rules and more transparent pricing.

latest.title: Digital Word of Mouth and Brand Trust
latest.venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
latest.abstract: The increasing expansion of social media, E-commerce and review websites has transformed how consumers look for and share information related to brands. Complementarily, eWOM — digital word-of-mouth — is consumer driven discussions regarding products, services, brands and companies that work through digital platforms. In contrast with the conventional word-of-mouth, communications shared via the digital medium can rapidly spread to a large audience and still remain accessible for a longer period This review discusses about some of the existing studies available on digital word-of-mouth, brand trust and consumer behaviour. Precisely , the review pays heavy attention on the online reviews, information authenticity, positive and negative eWOM, purchase intention and buyer behaviour. Previous studies indicate that the quality and usefulness of eWOM can influence consumer information and purchasing decisions , Nonetheless the effect of Ewom may also depend on the quality and characteristics of te information. The Research indicates that consumer trust and buying intentions can be influenced by how a brand reacts to negative reviews. The review highlights that digital word-of-mouth has now been an important factor into the consumer decision-making process and the authenticity of the reviews and also talks about the fake reviews and their impacts.

latest.title: Co-designing with Generative AI: consumer participation behaviour and product authenticity
latest.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping consumer–brand interactions, with fashion brands increasingly adopting Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) co-design tools that enable direct consumer participation in product design. This research examines how consumers evaluate the authenticity of the GenAI co-designed products, and how evaluation influences consumers’ future participation with fashion brands. This study further investigates whether consumer self-efficacy and perceived expertise toward the tools serve as key antecedents of the authenticity perceptions. By focusing on an emerging AI-enabled service (GenAI) context, this study expands consumer participation and value co-creation research by offering new insight into the drivers and consequences of the perceived authenticity of the fashion products co-created by GenAI and consumers.

latest.title: A consumer neuroscience approach to examining how augmented reality and QR codes support product and brand sustainability communication in retail settings
latest.abstract: This research explores the use of Augmented Reality (AR) and Quick Response (QR) codes as tools for communicating sustainability-related information in a quasi-realistic retail setting. It combines neurophysiological and self-report measures to investigate how these technologies influence consumers’ sustainability perceptions, emotional engagement, and cognitive workload. Participants took part in a simulated shopping experience, where they were exposed to one of three experimental conditions: traditional packaging, smartphone-mediated QR code scanning, and smartphone-mediated Augmented Reality exploration of coffee packaging. Cognitive workload (measured via electroencephalography) and emotional engagement (measured via skin conductance and heart rate) were recorded alongside self-report measures of green company orientation (GCO), green product informativeness (GPI), and brand familiarity. Findings indicate that while both AR and QR codes evoke more positive emotions and lead to higher perceptions of GCO and GPI, AR usage is also associated with higher cognitive workload. Additionally, brand familiarity enhanced self-report scores but not neurophysiological ones, without interacting with the interaction modality. This research provides a multi-level (implicit neurophysiological and explicit self-reported) perspective on the impact of digital packaging formats on sustainability communication. The findings contribute to ongoing discussions on how interactive technologies can support effective communication, implicit emotions, and consumer engagement with sustainability in retail environments.

latest.title: Different Strokes for Different Folks: Exploring Algorithmic Fairness and Trust in Generative Artificial Intelligence
latest.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely used to personalize recommendations, yet questions remain about the representativeness of algorithmic recommendations to recognize diverse consumer needs. This research integrates the stimulus‐organism‐response model and social identity theory to inform how personalization influences recommendation acceptance through algorithmic fairness and trust and how communication style affects these processes, which may differ between ethnic groups. Using a sequential explanatory design, Study 1 ( n = 136) shows that high personalization increases recommendation acceptance, perceived algorithmic fairness and trust compared with low personalization based on an experiment. Study 2 ( n = 300) identifies a positive sequential indirect effect through algorithmic fairness and trust, with competence‐oriented communication producing a stronger effect than warmth‐oriented communication based on an experiment. Study 3 ( n = 340) further reveals differences in these relationships across ethnic groups using a quasi‐experiment. Study 4 ( n = 14) employs semi‐structured interviews to contextualize these findings and explore the underlying reasoning. Theoretically, the findings extend GenAI personalization literature by identifying fairness and trust as key pathways to recommendation acceptance and highlighting ethnic differences in these processes. Practically, the findings guide strategies for GenAI developers to create more equitable and context‐sensitive design across diverse consumers.

latest.title: AI Personalization and Travel Booking Intention in GenAI-Assisted Travel Planning: The Roles of Recommendation Relevance, Perceived Decision Autonomy, and Travel Decision Satisfaction
latest.venue: Advances in management and applied economics
latest.abstract: This study examines the relationships among AI personalization, recommendation relevance, perceived decision autonomy, travel decision satisfaction, and travel booking intention in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted travel planning. An online survey using convenience sampling yielded 348 valid responses from consumers in Taiwan aged 20 years and older with experience using GenAI for travel planning. Structural equation modeling was used to test seven hypotheses. The model demonstrated good fit, and six hypotheses were supported. AI personalization was positively associated with recommendation relevance and perceived decision autonomy. Recommendation relevance was positively associated with perceived decision autonomy, and both constructs were positively associated with travel decision satisfaction. The direct association between perceived decision autonomy and travel booking intention was not significant after accounting for travel decision satisfaction. The path from travel decision satisfaction to travel booking intention had the largest standardized coefficient. These findings distinguish perceived personalization from recommendation relevance and clarify the different roles of autonomy and satisfaction in travel decision-making. For practitioners, the findings suggest that tourism platforms and GenAI service providers should offer recommendations aligned with consumers’ needs, preserve their autonomy over choices, and improve the decision-making experience. The study provides evidence to inform the design of GenAI travel recommendation services. JEL classification numbers: D12, L83, O33. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence, AI personalization, Perceived decision autonomy, Travel booking intention.

latest.title: Understanding digital purchase intentions: trust, scarcity marketing, and fomo among generation z
latest.venue: ECOBIZTECH Journal of Economics Business and Technology
latest.abstract: Purpose: to analyze the effects of trust, scarcity marketing, and fear of missing out (fomo) on generation z's purchase intention toward tiktok live shopping in Kendal regency. Method: this study used a quantitative approach and a survey method involving 100 generation z respondents in Kendal regency who had watched tiktok live shopping within the previous three months. Respondents were selected through purposive and snowball sampling techniques. Primary data were collected using an online questionnaire with a five-point likert scale and analyzed using multiple linear regression with SPSS version 27. Data analysis included validity and reliability tests, classical assumption tests, and hypothesis testing (t-test, F-test, and adjusted R²). Findings: trust, scarcity marketing, and fomo have positive and significant effects on generation z's purchase intention toward tiktok live shopping. All three variables significantly influence purchase intention, with fomo and scarcity marketing showing stronger effects than trust. The findings highlight the importance of functional, conditional, and social values in shaping generation z's digital purchasing behavior. Implications: this study encourages businesses to build trust, apply transparent scarcity promotions, and strengthen social engagement to increase purchase intention. Originality: lies in integrating trust, scarcity marketing, and fomo within the consumption value theory framework to explain generation z's purchase intention toward tiktok live shopping in Kendal regency.

latest.title: AI as Psychological Surrogate in Consumer Search: A Conceptual Framework and Future Research Directions
latest.abstract: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.

latest.title: Time Pressure and Impulse Buying: The Mechanism of Limited-Time E-Commerce Promotions in Shaping Consumer Decision-Making
latest.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
latest.abstract: Time-limited offers are ubiquitous in online retail, and it is important to understand how they operate and the risks they pose. Drawing on behavioural economics and cognitive psychology, this study uses Tmall's Double-11, Pinduoduo's "flash sales" and Amazon Prime Day as examples, and argues that multi-modal interface signals, such as the countdown clock, real-time inventory, and transaction volume displayed, can narrow the window of consumer deliberation and encourage more impulsive purchases. Although such designs may improve conversion performance, they also create structural vulnerabilities, such as manufactured scarcity in the interface, consumer cognitive overload and irrational herd behaviour resulting in over-buying. When misused, the application of these interfaces can be a form of psychological coercion. To mitigate these risks, the paper suggests three solutions: adding standardised interface rules with independent third-party audits to remove false urgency; enhancing the chances of cooling off and reducing information overload on the pages; and reducing social-proof cues and including rational-consumption reminders to prevent unnecessary spending. The research is both theoretically and practically relevant in terms of balancing commercial efficiency with consumer protection, and it probably has long-term consequences in terms of the sustainability of the e-commerce industry.

latest.title: Too Old to Benefit From FinTech ? An Exploratory Study on Older Adults' Access to and Adoption of Robo‐Advice
latest.abstract: Robo‐advice has the potential to provide affordable financial advice to assist older adults with building and managing retirement income. Yet robo‐advice uptake among those aged 60 to 80 years is low, and little is known about how they engage with robo‐advice. Our study examines the drivers and barriers to robo‐advice access and adoption among older adults, and provides practical recommendations for industry and policymakers. Drawing on qualitative surveys and interviews with academic and industry experts familiar with the Australian financial advice landscape. We identify six core themes and their possible interrelationships, which likely affect older adults' access and adoption: robo‐advice design, digital and financial capabilities, trust, psychological comfort, regulatory deficiencies, and social influence. In integrating our findings with the technology acceptance and financial planning literature, we construct a conceptual framework that responds to calls for more comprehensive explanations of consumer behavior toward robo‐advice.

latest.title: Comparative Analysis Between Subscription Economy and Ownership: A New Consumer Behavioral Model
latest.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
latest.abstract: Subscription-based services are increasingly significant in today’s economy, offering ongoing value to consumers while ensuring consistent revenue for businesses. Understanding consumer behavior within this framework is crucial for improving service offerings and fostering customer loyalty. This study examines the key factors influencing consumer decisions in subscription-based services. Using an exploratory approach, both qualitative and quantitative data are analyzed to identify patterns and motivations behind consumer choices. The analysis focuses on the impact of pricing structures, service quality, engagement strategies, and psychological factors on purchasing behavior. The findings offer actionable insights for service providers, highlighting strategies to enhance customer acquisition and retention. This research emphasizes the complexity of consumer behavior in the subscription economy and provides guidance for developing more effective business strategies.

latest.title: The Bandwagon Effect and Cognitive Biases in Internet-Famous Restaurant Choice: A Mechanism of Distorted Consumer Decision-Making
latest.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
latest.abstract: The selection of dining venues increasingly relies on user-generated content (UGC) on local-life platforms. The check-in practice of internet-famous restaurants is not just a dining-related behavior anymore, but rather a dual behavior including experiential consumption and online identity performance. This paper examines how the bandwagon effect, compounded by three cognitive biases, shapes restaurant choice, drawing on publicly observable UGC from Xiaohongshu and Dianping. Unlike the previous studies, which mainly repeat the conclusion of conformity effect, the current paper makes a clear difference between the informational bandwagon, which is derived from genuine consumer experience, and the commercial bandwagon created by marketing activities. In addition, it reveals how representativeness bias, confirmation bias, and availability bias successively exert their effects at each stage of the entire consumer decision process: information exposure, preference formation, pre-consumption expectation formation, and post-purchase feedback. However, it generates systematic mistakes in decision-making as well. Commercial bandwagon signals and the cognitive biases they exploit distort dining choices, inflate expectations, and misallocate capital. The paper proposes a three-party remedy: consumer psychological literacy, platform governance reform, and a merchant reorientation toward core-product value. The study extends consumer-behavior theory and yields operational guidance for sustaining the local catering market.

latest.title: Ảnh hưởng của video được tạo bởi AI trên TikTok đến ý định mua hàng trực tuyến của thế hệ Gen Z tại Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
latest.venue: Technical Education Science/Giáo dục Kỹ thuật
latest.abstract: Mặc dù nội dung do trí tuệ nhân tạo tạo ra (AIGC) đang bùng nổ tại thị trường Việt Nam, các nghiên cứu hiện hành chủ yếu tập trung vào các lĩnh vực chung mà chưa nhắm tới nền tảng cụ thể là TikTok. Do đó, vẫn còn khoảng trống nghiên cứu về định dạng video AI ngắn trên TikTok. Dựa trên khung lý thuyết SOR, nghiên cứu này đánh giá tác động của năm đặc tính video AI (tính xác thực, giải trí, thông tin, cá nhân hóa và rủi ro cảm nhận) đến ý định mua hàng trực tuyến của Gen Z thông qua vai trò trung gian là thái độ đối với video AI. Dữ liệu thu thập từ 251 người dùng tại Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh được xử lý thông qua việc đo lường PLS-SEM trên phần mềm SmartPLS 4 và hồi quy trung gian bằng PROCESS Macro (Bootstrap 5.000 mẫu). Kết quả cho thấy cả năm yếu tố đều có tác động ý nghĩa đến thái độ, trong đó tính giải trí và tính xác thực là hai động lực thúc đẩy mạnh mẽ nhất. Ngược lại, rủi ro cảm nhận lại tạo ra rào cản tiêu cực. Đáng chú ý là thái độ đóng vai trò trung gian một phần đối với tính xác thực, giải trí, thông tin, và trung gian hoàn toàn đối với tính cá nhân hóa và rủi ro cảm nhận. Nghiên cứu đóng góp vào lý thuyết hành vi người tiêu dùng số và cung cấp hàm ý chiến lược về ứng dụng AI trong truyền thông, định hướng đào tạo kỹ năng số và quản trị rủi ro công nghệ.

latest.title: Emotion Driven Biases in Consumer Decision Making: A Study on Cross Border Hand Made Y2K Retro Jewellery Consumption
latest.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
latest.abstract: Against a backdrop of intensifying cross-cultural exchange, emotion-driven decision-making bias is particularly salient in the rapidly expanding market for cross-border Y2K retro handmade jewellery. Integrating the affect-heuristic perspective and cross-cultural consumption frameworks, grounded in the affect heuristic—which posits that affective reactions serve as informational shortcuts in judgment—and cross-cultural consumption theory, this article investigates how combined emotions of nostalgia, exotic curiosity and identity -seeking produce consumer cognitive biases and various corresponding market outcomes. The current research points out both the positive functions, such as the promotion of cultural diversity and the empowerment of micro-creators, with three important issues: the distortions of the willingness to pay due to over-estimation of emotions, misinterpretations of cross-cultural aesthetics causing substantial returns, and impulsive spending amplified by social media. The study has also developed some solutions, including the application of ethical norms in marketing, visualization tools based on AR technologies, and the education of consumers in digital emotional literacy. The research has extended the affect-heuristic approach beyond the context of domestic retail by applying it to the sphere of transnational consumption and offered useful solutions for artisans, platforms, and lawmakers aimed at developing proper approaches to promote cross-national trade, which support sustainable retro shopping activities.

latest.title: Marketing d'influence et comportement omnicanal du consommateur : rôle médiateur de la confiance envers les enseignes de grande distribution au Maroc
latest.venue: International Journal of Research in Economics and Finance
latest.abstract: Cette étude analyse la manière dont le marketing d’influence et l’engagement communautaire sur les réseaux sociaux contribuent au comportement omnicanal des consommateurs marocains, en examinant le rôle médiateur de la confiance envers les enseignes de grande distribution. Dans une démarche hypothético-déductive, le modèle intègre le marketing d’influence comme construit composite d’ordre supérieur, composé de cinq dimensions (crédibilité, expertise, attractivité, congruence influenceur–enseigne et interactivité), ainsi que l’engagement communautaire, la confiance envers l’enseigne et le comportement omnicanal. Sept hypothèses sont évaluées auprès de 280 consommateurs marocains qui suivent des influenceurs et fréquentent des enseignes de grande distribution. Les données sont analysées avec SPSS 26, SmartPLS 4.0 (PLS-SEM) et Stata 17, cette dernière analyse servant de test de robustesse par régression logistique. Cinq hypothèses sont soutenues. L’effet direct du marketing d’influence sur le comportement omnicanal (H4) et l’effet modérateur de la fréquence d’exposition sur la relation entre marketing d’influence et confiance (H7) ne sont pas statistiquement significatifs. La régression logistique suggère toutefois un effet direct résiduel et modeste du marketing d’influence sur la décision d’adopter un parcours omnicanal. Le modèle explique 56,4 % de la variance de la confiance et 48,6 % de celle du comportement omnicanal. Ces résultats soulignent le rôle de la confiance dans la conversion des interactions avec les influenceurs en comportements entre canaux et éclairent les choix de collaboration des enseignes de grande distribution.

latest.title: From interpretation to rumination: An essay on integrating the self
latest.abstract: In response to Gruica’s paper, the essay reflects on the depressive rumination through established theories of negative thought repetition and my own interdisciplinary philosophical concept in the development, named Implosion oh Hyper- Significance which discusses how the possibility of creating meaning and significance can become burdensome because human natural cognitive drive tendency to interpret experiences and the world around them. Within this frame, depressive rumination can be considered as a manifestation of a broader interpretative process. This concept is not empirical, it is an example of the power of the metaphor in integrating self, precisely how reducing accumulated significance and finding one’s own interpretative concept can help the individual to understand their authentic identity better.

latest.title: Brand resilience under environmental threat: competing mediating roles of perceived value and environmental concern in seafood purchase intentions
latest.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how brand image shapes seafood purchase intentions under environmental threat. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response (S–O–R) framework, it examines the competing mediating roles of perceived value and environmental concern. Design/methodology/approach Using a systematic sampling approach, this study collected 319 valid questionnaires from coastal consumers in Guangdong Province, China. Structural equation modeling was used to test the dual-mediation model involving perceived value and environmental concern. Findings Brand image positively influences both perceived value and environmental concern. Perceived value enhances purchase intention, while environmental concern suppresses it. Both variables significantly mediate the brand–purchase relationship in opposing directions, with an overall positive indirect effect, suggesting that brand resilience endures despite ecological concerns. Originality/value This study contributes by modeling competing psychological mediators in seafood consumption under environmental threat, an area that has received limited attention in existing literature. It reveals consumer ambivalence during ecological crises: while strong brands retain appeal, environmental risk awareness weakens purchasing confidence. The findings offer actionable insights for seafood marketers on sustaining brand resilience through value communication and transparent sustainability practices.

latest.title: Religiosity and consumer behaviour among Millennials and Gen Z: does gender make a difference?
latest.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how religiosity is associated with consumer behaviour among Millennials and Gen Z in a highly religious emerging market. It proposes the spiritual cognitive consumption theory (SCCT), a dual pathway framework, and provides preliminary empirical support for its overall predictive validity. However, these two pathways were not directly measured; future experimental research is needed to isolate each mechanism. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 400 Nigerian respondents were analysed using structural equation modelling. Gender significantly moderates this relationship: women tend to show a stronger association between religiosity and relational aspects (e.g. brand trust, emotional congruity), whereas men focus more on instrumental outcomes (e.g. product functionality, religious symbolism). Findings The SCCT framework provides a nuanced understanding of the tension between spiritual devotion and market-based consumption. The findings offer marketers gender-sensitive, faith-conscious strategies and position SCCT as a robust theoretical tool for understanding spirituality, cognition and consumption in evolving digital economies. Social implications The study contributes to sustainable development goal (SDG) 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) by providing insights into inclusive, faith-sensitive marketing practices in the Global South. Originality/value The originality of this study lies in the development of the SCCT framework, which integrates spirituality, cognition and consumption into a dual pathway model. This offers a novel theoretical lens for understanding consumer behaviour in religious emerging markets.

latest.title: Exploring Traditional and Contemporary Retail Factors Shaping Customer Perceptions of Organised Retailing in Thanjavur District, Tamil Nadu
latest.venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
authors: S. Rashiya and Dr. T. Priyanga
latest.abstract: Organised retailing in India’s semi-urban and district-level markets is shaped by both established store-based attributes and emerging technology-enabled attributes. This study identifies and empirically validates the traditional and contemporary factors that shape customer perception of organised retailing in Thanjavur District, Tamil Nadu. Data were collected from 536 respondents using a structured questionnaire comprising 40 traditional-factor items and 20 contemporary-factor items, together with measures of customer perception, satisfaction, loyalty and repurchase intention. Following data screening, reliability analysis, sampling-adequacy diagnostics and exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation were performed on the 60 traditional and contemporary items. The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin value (.853) and Bartlett’s test of sphericity (χ² = 9,898.742, df = 1,770, p < .001) confirmed the suitability of the data for factor analysis. Parallel analysis supported the retention of eight empirical factors, which together explained 45.62 per cent of the total variance and demonstrated acceptable-to-good internal consistency (α = .648 to .866). In line with the analysis, the originally hypothesised thirteen sub-dimensions eight traditional and five contemporary were not empirically reproduced; instead, the items regrouped into a more defensible eight-factor structure that largely separated traditional store-based attributes from contemporary technology-enabled attributes. The findings indicate that customer perception of organised retailing in this district-level market is multidimensional, but is better represented by a re-specified, data-driven factor structure than by the original conceptual framework. The exploratory analysis resulted in an empirically derived eight-factor

latest.title: One City, Two Kinds of Time: Why Warehouse Clubs and Community Hard Discounters Can Coexist in Shanghai
latest.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
latest.abstract: Taking the juxtaposition of Sam's Club and Aldi in Shanghai as a case, this paper asks how two almost opposite retail models can take root and earn a profit in the same city. Existing explanations appeal to purchasing power, to format positioning, or to the capabilities of foreign firms. This paper proposes a three-part structure of time, space and symbol. Sam's Club sells "two hours of the weekend"; Aldi sells "fifteen minutes after work." The first rests on the car-borne ring beyond the outer ring road, the second on the walkable ring inside it. The first manufactures institutional trust — "I chose the right system" — through a membership card; the second manufactures price transparency — "I was not taken in" — through the price tag. The three structures reinforce one another and jointly lower the consumer's cost of choosing. Shanghai can hold both kinds of time not because it is richer but because four conditions hold at once: a thick and continuous middle in the income distribution, a sharply layered urban space, a supply chain in the Yangtze River Delta close at hand, and small, ageing households that arrived earlier than elsewhere. The paper further argues that the two firms are not each other's principal rival. Their common opponent is a retail environment of low price, low quality and low trust, and their boundary lies not in format but in whether a city still contains enough people willing to pay for certainty. Author: Ao Zhang, independent researcher; MA, Communication and Media Studies, Monash University. Data and disclaimer: Data as of 4 November 2026. Amounts in RMB unless otherwise stated. This is independent research; it does not constitute investment advice.

latest.title: Can the outcomes of transparent packaging be measured? A primary attempt at item screening
latest.abstract: Packaging has a significant impact on consumer choice and product purchase. Since almost all studies in this field have been conducted experimentally, this study aims to identify appropriate items to measure the outcomes of packaging transparency so that future researchers can use it in descriptive survey studies. This study was conducted using a mixed method (qualitative-quantitative) with the opinions of marketing and packaging experts. Concepts related to the meaning of transparent packaging were extracted from related studies using content analysis in the qualitative stage. Then, an online questionnaire was designed, and its link was provided to the panel members. Eleven concepts that expressed packaging transparency were extracted in the qualitative section, of which nine items were finally used in the quantitative section in the form of a questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Excel. Lawshe’s (1975) content validity ratio (CVR) method was used to assess the usefulness of the items, and five items were identified as suitable for measuring the outcomes of packaging transparency. These items relate to the visibility of the packaging contents, trust in product quality, willingness to purchase, preference for seeing the actual contents rather than an image on the package, and preference for buying products with transparent packaging.

latest.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Marketing Strategies for Enhancing Sales Conversion in E-Commerce: An Empirical and Analytical Investigation
latest.abstract: The rapid expansion of global e-commerce has intensified competition for consumer attention, rendering traditional demographic-segmented and rule-based marketing increasingly ineffective. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in digital marketing, enabling firms to process high-velocity behavioral datasets and deliver hyper-personalized customer journeys in real time. While industry adoption of AI marketing tools is widespread, a substantial maturity gap persists between experimental deployment and fully scaled conversion optimization. This paper integrates a multi-stage analytical research design—combining psychometric Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) of consumer survey data ($N = 420$), econometric before-and-after funnel cohort modeling across retail deployments, and regression-based moderation analysis—to quantify how AI-enabled digital marketing drives sales conversion. Specifically, the study examines four core strategic pillars: neural recommendation engines, predictive programmatic acquisition, dynamic pricing optimization, and generative conversational AI. Analytical results demonstrate that Perceived Personalization significantly enhances Customer Experience Quality ($\beta = 0.499, p < 0.001$) and Digital Marketing Effectiveness ($\beta = 0.488, p < 0.001$), which jointly mediate downstream Purchase Intention and actual checkout conversion ($R^2 = 0.412$). Econometric cohort tracking further reveals a 23.4% to 31.0% relative lift in session-to-purchase conversion rates, a 27% reduction in bounce rates, and up to a 50% increase in Average Order Value (AOV) via real-time affinity bundling. However, moderation analysis confirms that perceived algorithmic opacity and privacy intrusion negatively attenuate conversion gains ($\

latest.title: An Examination of Key Organizational Drivers, Strategic Leadership Practices and Best Practices for Enhancing Organizational Effectiveness
latest.abstract: This qualitative study explores the key drivers and best practices for building a strong organizational culture within private sector organizations in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada. Recognizing that organizational culture significantly influences employee engagement, performance, and retention, the research seeks to understand how culture is formed, sustained, and adapted in contemporary work environments. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with 18 professionals occupying leadership, HR, and managerial roles across six private organizations. Using thematic analysis, six core themes emerged: Leadership Influence, Recruitment and Cultural Fit, Recognition and Motivation, Culture in Hybrid Work Models, Technology and Culture Transmission, and Feedback Loops and Culture Assessment. The findings highlight the central role of leadership in modeling and reinforcing cultural values, the importance of value-based recruitment in maintaining cultural coherence, and the critical need for recognition systems that reflect organizational priorities. Additionally, the study reveals how hybrid work and digital platforms have redefined cultural expression and interaction. Regular feedback mechanisms emerged as vital tools for assessing and refining culture in dynamic business contexts. This study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on organizational behavior by offering practical recommendations for cultivating resilient and high-performing workplace cultures. It also identifies areas for future research, including sector-specific analysis, longitudinal studies, and quantitative validation of cultural indicators.
